q1.attribution: —Historian's account of the causes of the New Imperialism, c. 1870–1914
q1.directions: Use the passage below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Describe ONE motive for the New Imperialism described in the passage.
parts.b: Explain ONE cause of the speed of the Scramble for Africa after 1880.
parts.c: Explain ONE difference between British and French colonial administration in Africa.

sample_answers.a: One motive was economic: industrial economies sought raw materials such as rubber, minerals, and palm oil, plus protected markets, during the depression of the 1870s–90s.
sample_answers.b: One cause was the Berlin Conference of 1884–85, which set ground rules based on 'effective occupation' that turned competition into a race: once one power claimed territory, rivals rushed to claim their share before the map filled up.
sample_answers.c: The British generally ruled through indirect rule, keeping African chiefs and institutions under British residents to cut costs, while the French pursued direct rule and assimilation, replacing local rulers with French administrators.

q1.stimulus: Historians argue over why Europe partitioned Africa so suddenly after 1880. Economic explanations point to the search for raw materials and markets in an age of depression and tariff wars. Strategic explanations point to the Suez Canal, coaling stations, and the naval arms race. And cultural explanations point to Social Darwinism, missionary zeal, and the prestige of empire. Most now agree no single motive suffices: a French deputy wanted glory, a Belgian king wanted profit, and a British voter wanted both.

q2.attribution: —Adapted from Jules Ferry, French premier, speech to the Chamber of Deputies, 1885
q2.directions: Use the passage below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Identify ONE justification Ferry offers for colonial expansion.
parts.b: Explain ONE way Ferry's speech reflects European attitudes of the 1880s.
parts.c: Explain ONE way colonized peoples challenged the claims made in speeches like Ferry's.

sample_answers.a: Ferry claims that 'higher races' have both a right and a duty to rule and 'civilize' supposedly inferior peoples.
sample_answers.b: The speech reflects the fusion of racism and nationalism in the 1880s — Social Darwinist ideas about racial hierarchy joined to the belief that a great power proved itself by possessing colonies.
sample_answers.c: Colonized peoples challenged these claims through resistance and argument: Ethiopian armies defeated Italy at Adwa in 1896, and African and Asian intellectuals exposed the gap between the 'civilizing mission' and the violence of conquest.

q2.stimulus: The higher races have a right over the lower races. They have a duty to civilize the inferior races. I repeat that France must spread its language, its customs, and its flag wherever it can.

q3.attribution: Animated map of the colonization of Africa, 1880–1914
q3.directions: Use the map below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Describe ONE pattern shown on the map.
parts.b: Explain ONE technological development that made the rapid partition shown on the map possible.
parts.c: Explain ONE continuity in African resistance to colonial rule between the conquest period and the 1950s.

sample_answers.a: The map shows European control expanding from coastal footholds in 1880 to cover nearly the entire continent by 1914, with only Ethiopia and Liberia remaining independent.
sample_answers.b: One development was the steam gunboat and the Maxim gun: shallow-draft steamers carried European firepower up African rivers, and machine guns let small colonial forces defeat much larger African armies.
sample_answers.c: Africans resisted from the start and never stopped — from Samori Touré's wars against France in the 1880s–90s to the Mau Mau uprising and the Algerian war of the 1950s, armed and political resistance continued across the whole colonial period.

q3.stimulus: Animated map showing the colonization of Africa from 1880 to 1914: European-controlled territory spreads across the continent until nearly all of Africa is partitioned among Britain, France, Germany, Portugal, Belgium, and Italy.
